title: Automatic investing at big brokerages
fact: Fidelity, Charles Schwab and Vanguard all let customers schedule automatic recurring investments into mutual funds or ETFs, and Fidelity and Schwab offer fractional shares, so even small amounts buy part of an S&P 500 fund.
say: "We'd automate it: a recurring transfer into an S&P 500 index fund at a brokerage like Fidelity the day after payday, so money that would sit idle starts working right away."
source: Fidelity, Schwab and Vanguard account features
answers: How will our client stick with the plan?
How can our client start investing with little money?

title: What the S&P 500 has actually returned
fact: From 1928 through 2025 the S&P 500 compounded at roughly 10% a year including dividends, or about 7% after inflation. Single years swing widely: about -37% in 2008 and about -18% in 2022.
say: "Historically the S&P 500 has averaged about 10% a year since 1928. That's an average, not a promise: in 2008 it fell 37%, which is why this is money for five years or more."
source: NYU Stern (Damodaran) historical returns data; S&P Dow Jones Indices
answers: What return can our client expect?
What if the market crashes right after they invest?

title: Rule of 72
fact: Divide 72 by an annual return to estimate how many years money takes to double: at 8% about 9 years, at 4% about 18 years.
say: "By the Rule of 72, at 8% your money doubles about every 9 years, so starting at 22 instead of 31 gives you one extra doubling."
answers: How fast will this money grow?
Why invest now instead of later?

title: Starting early beats investing more later
fact: $200 a month from age 22 to 65 at an 8% average return grows to about $895,000. The same $200 a month started at 32 grows to about $387,000.
say: "Waiting ten years cuts the result by more than half. Time is the most valuable thing a young investor has."
source: Future value of an annuity, calculated in this app
answers: Why should a young client invest now?

title: Index funds are cheap
fact: Broad index funds and ETFs from large providers commonly charge expense ratios under 0.10% a year, and Fidelity offers ZERO index funds with a 0% expense ratio. Many actively managed funds charge 0.5% to 1% or more.
say: "A low-cost index fund keeps more of the return in your pocket. A 1% fee can eat roughly a quarter of your money over 30 years."
source: Fund provider fee disclosures; SEC Investor.gov fee calculator
answers: Why an index fund instead of picking stocks?
How much do fees really matter?

title: Dollar-cost averaging
fact: Investing a fixed amount on a schedule buys more shares when prices fall and fewer when they rise, and removes the temptation to time the market.
say: "With dollar-cost averaging, a market dip becomes a sale: your same $300 buys more shares."
answers: Should our client invest all at once or spread it out?
What if the market drops right after they invest?

title: Target-date funds
fact: Target-date funds hold a stock and bond mix that automatically becomes more conservative as the target year nears. They are the default investment in many 401(k) plans.
say: "If you want one decision and done, a 2070 target-date fund diversifies and rebalances for you."
source: SEC Investor Bulletin on target date funds
answers: What's the simplest investment for a beginner?

title: High-yield savings rates right now
fact: In mid-November 2026, top online high-yield savings accounts paid about 4.35% APY (some with balance minimums), while many big-bank basic savings accounts pay far less.
say: "Your emergency fund shouldn't earn almost nothing. Top online savings accounts pay around 4% right now and are still FDIC-insured."
source: Bankrate best high-yield savings, rates as of 11/12/2026
answers: Where should the emergency fund go?
Why not just keep savings at a big bank?

title: Emergency fund guideline
fact: Most planners recommend 3 to 6 months of essential expenses in cash before investing beyond an employer match; single-income or commission-based households often aim for 6 or more.
say: "Step one is protection: three to six months of expenses in high-yield savings, so a car repair never becomes credit card debt."
answers: How much should our client keep in savings?
What should our client do first?

title: 50/30/20 budget
fact: A simple guideline: 50% of after-tax pay to needs, 30% to wants, 20% to savings and extra debt payments.
say: "We'd start with 50/30/20: it's simple enough to stick to and it guarantees 20% goes to your future."
source: Popularized by Sen. Elizabeth Warren's book 'All Your Worth' (2005)
answers: How should our client build a budget?

title: CDs and Treasury bills for short-term goals
fact: CDs lock a fixed rate for a set term with a penalty for early withdrawal. Treasury bills are short-term U.S. government debt (4 to 52 weeks), sold at TreasuryDirect.gov or through brokerages, and their interest is exempt from state income tax.
say: "For your house down payment in two years, we'd use a CD ladder or Treasury bills: safe, predictable, and not exposed to a stock market drop right before you buy."
answers: Where should money for a short-term goal go?

title: Stocks vs bonds in one line
fact: A stock is ownership in a company; a bond is a loan to a company or government that pays interest. Bonds are usually steadier; stocks have higher long-run returns and bigger swings.
say: "Stocks are for growth, bonds are for stability, and the mix depends on when you need the money."
answers: What's the difference between a stock and a bond?

title: 401(k) and IRA limits for 2026 and 2027
fact: 2026: 401(k) employee limit $24,500; IRA $7,500. 2027 (IRS Notice 2026-66, Nov. 12, 2026): 401(k) $25,500, catch-up for 50+ $8,500, higher catch-up of $11,750 for ages 60-63; IRA stays $7,500 with a $1,100 catch-up.
say: "Next year you can put up to $25,500 into your 401(k), and if you're over 50 another $8,500 on top."
answers: How much can our client put in a 401(k) or IRA?

title: The employer match is free money
fact: A common match is 50% or 100% of contributions up to 3% to 6% of salary. Not contributing enough to get the full match leaves part of your pay on the table.
say: "If your company matches 4%, contributing 4% is an instant 100% return. Nothing else in finance does that."
source: Typical plan design (Vanguard 'How America Saves' reports)
answers: What should our client do first with their paycheck?
Which job offer is better?

title: Roth vs traditional
fact: Traditional 401(k)/IRA: tax break now, taxed at withdrawal. Roth: contributions after tax, qualified withdrawals tax-free. Roth tends to win when your tax rate is low now (young workers).
say: "You're in a low tax bracket now, so paying tax today with a Roth and withdrawing tax-free later is the smart trade."
answers: Roth or traditional?

title: Auto-enrollment under SECURE 2.0
fact: SECURE 2.0 (2022) requires most new 401(k) and 403(b) plans started after Dec. 29, 2022 to automatically enroll workers beginning with plan years after 2024, at 3% to 10% with automatic yearly increases.
say: "Congress made automatic saving the default in new plans because it works: people who are auto-enrolled stay enrolled."
answers: How can a business help employees save?

title: Social Security timing
fact: You can claim Social Security from 62 to 70. Each year you wait past full retirement age (67 for anyone born 1960 or later) adds about 8% to your monthly benefit until 70.
say: "Delaying Social Security from 67 to 70 raises your check by roughly 24% for life."
answers: When should our client claim Social Security?

title: 529 plans
fact: 529 plans grow tax-free when used for qualified education expenses (college costs, plus K-12 tuition up to an annual cap). Many states give a state income tax deduction for contributions.
say: "A 529 plan for your daughter grows tax-free for college, and many states give you a tax break when you put money in."
source: IRS Publication 970; SEC Investor.gov on 529 plans
answers: How should parents save for college?

title: 529 to Roth IRA rollover
fact: Under SECURE 2.0, starting in 2024 unused 529 money can roll into the beneficiary's Roth IRA, up to $35,000 lifetime, if the 529 has been open at least 15 years, subject to annual Roth limits.
say: "If your child gets a scholarship, the money isn't stuck: up to $35,000 can roll into their Roth IRA."
answers: What if the child doesn't go to college?

title: Trump Accounts for newborns
fact: The 2025 tax law created Trump Accounts: children who are U.S. citizens born from 2025 through 2028 can get a one-time $1,000 federal seed deposit (claimed on IRS Form 4547). Contributions began July 4, 2026, up to $5,000 a year from family and others (employers up to $2,500 of that), invested in low-cost U.S. stock index funds. IRS rules were still proposed as of mid-2026.
say: "Because your baby was born this year, they qualify for a $1,000 government deposit in a Trump Account. We'd claim it right away and add to it every month."
source: One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025); IRS proposed regulations (May 2026); trumpaccounts.gov
answers: What accounts can new parents open for their baby?

title: FAFSA
fact: The Free Application for Federal Student Aid (studentaid.gov) unlocks federal grants, work-study and federal loans; many states and colleges use it for their own aid. File every year, as early as possible.
say: "Before borrowing a dollar, file the FAFSA: it's free and it's the key to grants you never repay."
answers: How can our client pay for college?

title: Annual gift tax exclusion
fact: In 2026 a person can give up to $19,000 to any one person without filing a gift tax return; a married couple can give $38,000 per recipient. The limit rises to $20,000 ($40,000 per couple) in 2027. A 529 allows five years of gifts at once ($95,000 in 2026).
say: "Grandparents can each give $19,000 a year per grandchild with no gift tax paperwork, and a 529 lets them front-load five years."
source: IRS annual exclusion for 2026; IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-35 for 2027
answers: How can grandparents help without tax problems?

title: Custodial Roth IRA for teens
fact: A teen with earned income (a part-time job) can have a custodial Roth IRA and contribute up to the lesser of their earnings or the annual limit.
say: "With your summer job income, you could open a custodial Roth IRA now and give that money 50 years to grow tax-free."
answers: How can a teenager start investing?

title: How much life insurance
fact: A common rule of thumb is coverage of 10 to 12 times annual income; the DIME method adds Debt, Income replacement, Mortgage and Education costs. Term life is far cheaper than whole life for the same coverage.
say: "For a new parent we'd look at term life of about 10 to 12 times income, a 20- or 30-year term to cover the years your child depends on you."
source: Common planning guidelines (e.g., LIMRA consumer research, insurer calculators)
answers: How much life insurance does our client need?

title: Disability insurance
fact: Long-term disability insurance usually replaces about 60% of income. The Social Security Administration estimates about 1 in 4 of today's 20-year-olds will become disabled before retirement age.
say: "Your ability to earn is your biggest asset. Disability coverage protects it: about 1 in 4 of today's 20-year-olds will face a disability before 67."
answers: What insurance does a young worker need?

title: Life events trigger a review
fact: Marriage, a new baby, buying a home, starting a business and a new job are the moments to review life, disability, health, property and liability coverage and update beneficiaries.
say: "A new baby is the number-one moment to review insurance and beneficiaries. We'd do it this month."
answers: How often should the client review their plan?

title: Umbrella liability
fact: Umbrella policies add liability coverage (often $1 million or more) above home and auto limits and are relatively inexpensive.
say: "As your net worth grows, an umbrella policy protects it from a lawsuit for roughly the cost of a streaming subscription a month."
answers: How can a wealthier client protect against lawsuits?

title: HSA limits for 2026 and 2027
fact: With a high-deductible health plan, HSA contribution limits are $4,400 (self-only) and $8,750 (family) for 2026, rising to $4,500 and $9,000 for 2027. HSAs are triple tax-advantaged: deductible in, tax-free growth, tax-free out for medical costs.
say: "If you have a high-deductible plan, the HSA is the best tax deal in the code: money goes in tax-free and comes out tax-free for medical bills."
source: IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-19 (2026) and Rev. Proc. 2026-24 (2027)
answers: How can our client save on health costs?

title: Four ways to handle risk
fact: Avoid it (don't do the activity), reduce/control it (safety steps, internal controls), transfer it (insurance, contracts), or retain/accept it (self-insure small losses).
say: "For each risk we'd decide: avoid it, reduce it, transfer it with insurance, or accept it. Here's which we chose and why."
answers: What's the biggest risk and how would you handle it?

title: Small business insurance basics
fact: Common coverages: general liability, commercial property, a business owner's policy (BOP) bundling both, professional liability, commercial auto, cyber, and workers' compensation (required in nearly every state once you have employees).
say: "We'd start with a business owner's policy and add workers' comp the day you hire your first employee."
answers: What insurance should this business buy?

title: What makes up a FICO score
fact: Payment history 35%, amounts owed (utilization) 30%, length of credit history 15%, new credit 10%, credit mix 10%.
say: "The two biggest levers are paying on time, 35% of your score, and keeping balances low, 30%."
answers: How can our client improve their credit score?

title: Utilization under 30%
fact: Using less than 30% of available credit is a widely cited guideline; people with the highest scores often use under 10%.
say: "Keep your card balance under 30% of the limit, and under 10% if you're about to apply for a mortgage."
answers: How should our client use credit cards responsibly?

title: Free credit reports and freezes
fact: AnnualCreditReport.com gives free weekly reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion (made permanent in 2023). Credit freezes have been free at all three bureaus since 2018.
say: "Check all three reports free every week at AnnualCreditReport.com, and freeze your credit for free so no one can open accounts in your name."
source: FTC; Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief and Consumer Protection Act (2018)
answers: How does our client check their credit?
How do we protect against identity theft?

title: Credit card interest is expensive
fact: Average interest rates on credit card accounts that pay interest have been above 20% in recent years, according to Federal Reserve G.19 data.
say: "Carrying a balance at over 20% APR wipes out any investment return, so we pay the card in full every month on autopay."
source: Federal Reserve G.19 Consumer Credit release
answers: Should our client pay off debt or invest first?

title: CARD Act protections
fact: The Credit CARD Act of 2009 requires 45 days' notice of major rate changes, limits fees, and requires statements to show how long paying only the minimum will take.
say: "Look at the minimum-payment box on your statement: the CARD Act requires it to show how many years minimums would take."
answers: What protections does a cardholder have?

title: Avalanche vs snowball
fact: Avalanche pays the highest interest rate first (saves the most); snowball pays the smallest balance first (quick wins that build motivation).
say: "Mathematically, the avalanche saves you the most interest. If you need early wins to stay motivated, the snowball works too."
answers: How should our client pay off debt?

title: Five Cs of credit
fact: Lenders judge Character, Capacity (ability to repay), Capital, Collateral and Conditions.
say: "A lender looks at the five Cs, so we'd strengthen capacity by lowering your debt-to-income ratio before you apply."
answers: What does a lender look at?

title: FDIC and NCUA insurance
fact: The FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category; the NCUA gives credit union members the same coverage. No depositor has lost a penny of FDIC-insured funds since the FDIC began in 1934.
say: "Your deposits are FDIC-insured up to $250,000. Since 1934 no one has lost a penny of insured deposits."
answers: Is our client's money safe at the bank?

title: SIPC protection at brokerages
fact: SIPC protects customers up to $500,000 (including $250,000 cash) if a member brokerage fails and assets are missing. It does not protect against market losses.
say: "If the brokerage itself failed, SIPC covers up to $500,000. Market drops aren't covered, which is why we diversify."
answers: What happens if a brokerage firm fails?

title: Silicon Valley Bank, 2023
fact: In March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank failed after depositors tried to withdraw about $42 billion in one day; most deposits were uninsured and the bank held long-term bonds that lost value when rates rose. Regulators protected all depositors.
say: "SVB shows two risks: keeping balances over the insurance limit, and a bank not managing interest-rate risk. We'd spread large balances across banks."
source: Federal Reserve review of SVB (April 2023); FDIC
answers: Why do banks fail?
How do we protect a large balance?

title: Synapse fintech collapse, 2024
fact: When banking-as-a-service middleman Synapse filed for bankruptcy in 2024, customers of several fintech apps had their money frozen because records of who owned what didn't match. FDIC insurance protects you if the bank fails, not if a fintech middleman fails.
say: "Before you trust an app with your savings, know which bank actually holds the money and whether you're covered if the app itself fails."
source: News coverage; FDIC consumer guidance on fintech
answers: Is money in a payment app insured?

title: Instant payments: FedNow and Zelle
fact: The Federal Reserve launched FedNow, an instant payment service for banks, in July 2023. Zelle, owned by seven large banks, moves money between U.S. bank accounts in minutes.
say: "Instant payments through FedNow and Zelle mean customers expect money to move in seconds, so the bank's app has to keep up."
answers: How should our client send money safely?

title: Credit unions vs banks
fact: Credit unions are not-for-profit cooperatives owned by members; they often offer lower loan rates and fees. Banks are usually for-profit and owned by shareholders, with larger branch and ATM networks.
say: "A credit union returns profits to members through better rates; a big bank offers more locations and services. It depends on what you value."
answers: Bank or credit union?

title: Fewer, bigger banks
fact: The number of FDIC-insured institutions has fallen from more than 14,000 in the mid-1980s to fewer than 4,500, mostly through mergers.
say: "Banking has consolidated dramatically: there are less than a third as many banks as in the 1980s."
answers: How does consolidation affect customers?

title: Recent consolidation deals
fact: JPMorgan Chase bought First Republic Bank after it failed in May 2023. Capital One completed its acquisition of Discover Financial in May 2025, combining a big card issuer with a payment network.
say: "Capital One buying Discover is a great example: a lender buying a payment network to control more of the value chain."
answers: Why do banks merge?

title: Convergence: Citigroup and Gramm-Leach-Bliley
fact: Citicorp (a bank) merged with Travelers Group (insurance and brokerage) in 1998 to form Citigroup. The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999 then legally allowed banks, securities firms and insurers to combine.
say: "Convergence means one company offering banking, investing and insurance, which became legal with Gramm-Leach-Bliley in 1999."
answers: What is convergence in the finance industry?

title: Federal funds rate
fact: The Fed raised its target range by 0.25 point to 3.75%-4.00% on Sept. 16, 2026 and held it there on Oct. 28, 2026 (10-2 vote; two members wanted another hike). The next meeting is Dec. 8-9, 2026.
say: "The Fed raised rates in September to fight inflation. That makes borrowing costlier but means savers can lock in about 4% safely right now."
source: Federal Reserve FOMC statements, Sept. 16 and Oct. 28, 2026
answers: How do the Fed's decisions affect our client?

title: Inflation
fact: Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September 2026, above the Fed's 2% target, driven in part by energy (gasoline spiked above $4.50 a gallon in spring 2026). October CPI rose 0.4% for the month; no 12-month figure was published for October because 2025 data were missing.
say: "With inflation near 3.7%, money in a 0.25% savings account loses buying power every year."
source: Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI releases, 2026
answers: How does inflation change your recommendation?

title: Mortgage rates
fact: The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was about 7.11% in Freddie Mac's survey for the week of Nov. 12, 2026 (15-year about 6.45%).
say: "Mortgage rates are around 7%, so improving your credit score before you buy could save you a lot over 30 years."
source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey
answers: Should our client buy a house now?

title: Bull, bear and correction
fact: A correction is a drop of about 10% from a recent high; a bear market is a drop of 20% or more; a bull market is a long rise. Recessions are officially dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research.
say: "Corrections of 10% happen often. Long-term investors plan for them instead of reacting to them."
answers: What if the market drops 20%?

title: Rates and bond prices move opposite
fact: When interest rates rise, prices of existing bonds fall, and long-term bonds fall the most. This is exactly what hurt Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
say: "Because rates rose, we'd favor shorter-term bonds and CDs so the client isn't locked into low rates."
source: SEC Investor.gov on interest rate risk
answers: Why do bond prices fall when rates rise?

title: Global investing and currency risk
fact: U.S. companies make up roughly 60% of global stock market value, so a U.S.-only portfolio skips a large part of the world. Foreign investments add currency risk: a stronger dollar lowers the value of foreign returns.
say: "Owning some international funds adds diversification, but returns move with exchange rates too."
source: MSCI All Country World Index country weights
answers: Should our client invest internationally?

title: Fiduciary vs best interest
fact: Registered investment advisers owe clients a fiduciary duty under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Broker-dealers must follow Regulation Best Interest (effective June 2020) when recommending investments to retail customers. CFP professionals must act as fiduciaries when giving financial advice.
say: "We act in your best interest, we disclose how we're paid, and we put every recommendation and its reasons in writing."
source: SEC (Advisers Act; Reg BI); CFP Board Code of Ethics
answers: What are your responsibilities to us?

title: Check any advisor yourself
fact: FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure site show licenses, employment history and disciplinary records. Investor.gov links to both.
say: "Don't take our word for it: look us up on FINRA BrokerCheck tonight and see our licenses and record."
answers: How can the client trust you?

title: Client privacy
fact: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act requires financial institutions to explain how they share customer information and to safeguard it (the Safeguards Rule).
say: "Your information is protected by federal privacy law, and we'll explain exactly who can see it."
answers: How will you protect my information?

title: Sarbanes-Oxley
fact: Passed in 2002 after Enron and WorldCom, Sarbanes-Oxley requires CEOs and CFOs to certify financial reports (Section 302), requires internal-control reporting and auditor attestation (Section 404), and created the PCAOB to oversee auditors.
say: "After Enron, Sarbanes-Oxley made executives personally sign off on the numbers. That's the standard we'd hold this company to."
answers: How do laws keep company reports honest?

title: Dodd-Frank and the CFPB
fact: The Dodd-Frank Act (2010), the response to the 2008 crisis, created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Financial Stability Oversight Council, stress tests for large banks, and the Volcker Rule.
say: "After 2008, Dodd-Frank created the CFPB so consumers have a regulator focused only on them."
source: Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act
answers: How do regulations protect consumers?

title: Wells Fargo fake accounts
fact: Wells Fargo employees opened millions of unauthorized accounts under aggressive sales goals (revealed in 2016). The bank paid $3 billion to settle criminal and civil cases in 2020 and $3.7 billion to the CFPB in 2022.
say: "Wells Fargo shows what happens when sales goals reward the wrong behavior. We'd measure client outcomes, not just products sold."
answers: Why does ethics matter in finance?

title: FTX fraud
fact: Crypto exchange FTX collapsed in November 2022 after customer funds were secretly used by an affiliated trading firm. Founder Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted of fraud in 2023 and sentenced to 25 years in 2024.
say: "FTX had no real board, no controls and customer money mixed with company money. Governance and segregation of funds matter."
answers: Should our client invest in crypto?

title: Ponzi warning signs
fact: Bernard Madoff's Ponzi scheme, exposed in 2008, involved about $65 billion in reported (fictitious) account value. Red flags: guaranteed or unusually steady high returns, secrecy, unregistered sellers, pressure to act fast.
say: "Anyone promising guaranteed high returns is a red flag. Madoff's steady returns were the tell."
answers: How can a client spot investment fraud?

title: Insider trading case
fact: Galleon Group founder Raj Rajaratnam was sentenced in 2011 to 11 years in prison for insider trading, one of the longest sentences for the crime.
say: "Trading on information the public doesn't have is illegal. Rajaratnam got 11 years."
answers: What's illegal in securities trading?

title: Anti-money-laundering rules
fact: Under the Bank Secrecy Act, banks file Currency Transaction Reports for cash transactions over $10,000 and Suspicious Activity Reports, and must verify customer identity (KYC).
say: "Compliance isn't red tape: KYC and transaction monitoring keep criminals out and protect the bank's reputation."
answers: How do banks stop money laundering?

title: Consumer fraud losses
fact: Consumers reported losing a record $15.9 billion to fraud in 2025, up about 25% from 2024, according to the FTC. Investment scams were the largest category at about $7.9 billion, nearly half the total.
say: "Fraud is growing fast: the FTC counted a record $15.9 billion in reported losses in 2025, so scam protection belongs in every plan."
answers: How big a problem is fraud?

title: Older adults are top targets
fact: The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center reported that people 60 and older lost about $4.9 billion to online fraud in 2024.
say: "Older clients are targeted most, so we'd add a trusted contact to your account and a verbal password with the bank."
answers: How would you protect an older client?

title: Occupational fraud
fact: The Association of Certified Fraud Examiners estimates organizations lose about 5% of revenue to fraud each year; tips are the most common way fraud is detected, and small businesses suffer high median losses.
say: "Fraud costs the typical organization about 5% of revenue. A tip line and separation of duties are the cheapest defenses."
source: ACFE Occupational Fraud Report to the Nations
answers: How would you prevent employee theft?

title: Multifactor authentication
fact: Microsoft has reported that multifactor authentication blocks more than 99% of automated account-compromise attacks. Authenticator apps or passkeys are stronger than text-message codes.
say: "Turning on multifactor authentication stops almost all automated account takeovers."
answers: How should our client secure online accounts?

title: Benford's Law
fact: In many naturally occurring financial data sets, about 30% of numbers start with 1 and fewer than 5% start with 9. Auditors use this to spot made-up numbers.
say: "We'd run a Benford's Law test on expense data: fabricated numbers rarely follow the natural pattern."
answers: How can data analysis catch fraud?

title: How many new businesses survive
fact: About 1 in 5 new U.S. businesses close within their first year and roughly half within five years.
say: "About half of new businesses don't reach year five, usually because of cash flow, so we'd build a cash budget before you open."
source: Bureau of Labor Statistics Business Employment Dynamics
answers: What's the biggest risk for this new business?

title: SBA loans
fact: SBA 7(a) loans go up to $5 million; SBA microloans go up to $50,000 through nonprofit intermediaries. The SBA guarantees part of the loan, making lenders more willing to lend.
say: "An SBA microloan of up to $50,000 fits a start-up like yours, and the government guarantee helps a new business qualify."
answers: How should this business get funding?

title: Business structures
fact: Sole proprietorship: simplest, unlimited personal liability. Partnership: shared ownership, needs a partnership agreement. LLC: limited liability with pass-through taxes. S corp: pass-through taxation, up to 100 shareholders. C corp: separate taxpayer, can raise money by selling stock.
say: "For you and your friend, an LLC with a written operating agreement protects your personal assets and spells out what happens if one of you leaves."
answers: What form of ownership do you recommend?

title: Profit is not cash
fact: A business can be profitable on its income statement and still run out of cash if customers pay late, inventory piles up or loan payments are due. That's why a cash flow budget matters.
say: "Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact: we'd build a 13-week cash forecast so you see a crunch before it hits."
answers: Why is a profitable business short on cash?

title: Small business finance tools
fact: Cloud accounting software such as QuickBooks Online and Xero connects to bank accounts, automates bookkeeping and produces income statements, balance sheets and cash flow reports; payroll tools like Gusto handle tax withholding.
say: "With QuickBooks or Xero linked to your bank, your financial statements update themselves and your accountant sees the same numbers you do."
answers: How would you use technology to manage the business's money?

title: Ratios lenders check
fact: Current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities; above 1.5 is generally healthy), debt-to-equity, net profit margin, and debt service coverage (operating cash flow ÷ debt payments; lenders often look for 1.25 or more).
say: "Banks want to see your cash flow cover loan payments at least 1.25 times, so we'd show them that number up front."
answers: How do you know if the business is healthy?

title: Board independence
fact: NYSE and Nasdaq listing rules require a majority of independent directors and a fully independent audit committee. Separating the CEO and board chair roles adds oversight.
say: "Investors want an independent board and audit committee; that's a listing requirement and it raises what investors will pay."
source: NYSE Listed Company Manual 303A; Nasdaq Rule 5605
answers: What makes a well-governed company?

title: WeWork's failed 2019 IPO
fact: WeWork withdrew its 2019 IPO after investors objected to governance problems, including the founder's outsized voting control and conflicts of interest; the company later filed for bankruptcy in 2023.
say: "WeWork proves governance affects value: investors walked away from the IPO because one person controlled everything."
answers: Why does governance matter to investors?

title: COSO frameworks
fact: COSO's Internal Control-Integrated Framework (2013) and Enterprise Risk Management framework (2017) are the most widely used standards for internal control and ERM.
say: "We'd follow the COSO framework so risks are managed across the whole company, not in silos."
answers: What is enterprise risk management?

title: AI in financial services
fact: Banks and card networks use machine learning to score transactions for fraud in real time, and many firms use AI to answer customer questions and summarize documents, with human review for decisions.
say: "AI can flag suspicious transactions in milliseconds, but a person should review any decision that affects a customer."
answers: What are the risks of banks using AI?

title: Sustainability reporting
fact: The International Sustainability Standards Board issued IFRS S1 and S2 in 2023 as a global baseline for sustainability and climate-related disclosures, and several countries are adopting them.
say: "Investors increasingly ask for sustainability data next to financial results, so we'd report a few key measures now."
answers: How can financial information be used beyond accounting?

title: Finance careers and credentials
fact: CFP (financial planning), CPA (accounting), CFA (investment analysis), and FINRA licenses such as the Series 7 and 66 for brokers and advisers. Personal financial advisors earned a median of roughly $100,000 a year in recent BLS data.
say: "Our team would include a CFP for planning and a CPA for tax questions, so every part of your plan is covered."
source: Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook; CFP Board; FINRA
answers: What finance career interests you, and why?

title: 2027 tax brackets and standard deduction
fact: For 2027 the standard deduction rises to $16,600 for single filers, $33,200 for married couples filing jointly and $24,925 for heads of household. The seven rates (10% to 37%) stay the same and bracket thresholds rise about 3.2% for inflation.
say: "For 2027 the first $16,600 of a single filer's income isn't taxed at all, thanks to the standard deduction."
answers: Will a raise push our client into a higher tax bracket?
How much of our client's income is actually taxed?

title: No tax on tips and overtime (2025-2028)
fact: Under the 2025 tax law, workers can deduct up to $25,000 of qualified tips and up to $12,500 of overtime premium pay ($25,000 for joint filers) from federal income tax for 2025 through 2028, with phase-outs at higher incomes. Social Security and Medicare taxes still apply.
say: "Your tips are now deductible from federal income tax through 2028, but you still owe payroll tax on them, so we'll set that aside."
source: IRS guidance on the 2025 tax law
answers: How does our client's job income get taxed?
How should a tipped worker budget?

title: Extra $6,000 senior deduction
fact: For 2025 through 2028, taxpayers 65 and older can claim an extra deduction of up to $6,000 each ($12,000 for a qualifying couple), phased out for higher incomes, on top of the regular standard deduction.
say: "Because you're over 65, you get an extra $6,000 deduction through 2028, which lowers the tax on your retirement withdrawals."
source: IRS guidance on the 2025 tax law
answers: How can a retired client lower taxes on withdrawals?

title: Child tax credit: $2,200 per child
fact: The 2025 tax law set the child tax credit at $2,200 per qualifying child and indexed it to inflation. A credit cuts the tax bill dollar for dollar.
say: "Your new baby brings a $2,200 tax credit each year, money we can send straight into the 529."
answers: What's the difference between a deduction and a credit?
How can new parents find money to save?

title: Charity deduction without itemizing (from 2026)
fact: Starting in tax year 2026, people who take the standard deduction can still deduct up to $1,000 ($2,000 for married couples) of cash gifts to qualifying charities.
say: "Starting this year, your $1,000 of donations is deductible even though you don't itemize."
source: IRS guidance on the 2025 tax law
answers: How can our client give to charity on a tight budget?

title: Long-term vs short-term capital gains
fact: Gains on assets held more than a year are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%; gains on assets held a year or less are taxed as ordinary income, up to 37%. Losses can offset gains, plus up to $3,000 of other income a year.
say: "Waiting until you've held it over a year moves the gain from your 22% rate to 15%."
answers: How do taxes affect when our client sells investments?

title: Car loan interest deduction (2025-2028)
fact: For 2025 through 2028, interest on a loan for a new vehicle assembled in the U.S. is deductible up to $10,000 a year, phased out at higher incomes.
say: "If you buy a new U.S.-assembled car, part of the loan interest is deductible through 2028, but a cheaper car still saves more."
source: IRS guidance on the 2025 tax law
answers: Should our client finance a new car?

title: Social Security for 2027
fact: Benefits rise 3.6% starting January 2027. The maximum wage subject to Social Security tax rises from $184,500 to $192,300; the 6.2% employee tax is capped at $11,922.60. Medicare's 1.45% has no cap.
say: "Social Security benefits rise 3.6% in January because of inflation. It's one of the few retirement incomes that keeps pace automatically."
answers: Will Social Security keep up with inflation?
Why is our client's paycheck smaller than expected?

title: Saver's Match starts in 2027
fact: Under SECURE 2.0, starting in 2027 eligible lower- and moderate-income workers who contribute to a retirement account get a federal matching deposit of 50% of contributions, up to $1,000 a year.
say: "Starting in 2027, the government will match half of your retirement contributions, up to $1,000 a year, if you qualify."
answers: How can a lower-income client afford to save for retirement?

title: Social Security's 2033 shortfall
fact: The 2025 Social Security Trustees Report projected the retirement trust fund would be depleted in 2033; after that, incoming payroll taxes could pay about 77% of scheduled benefits unless Congress acts.
say: "Social Security isn't going away, but it may pay about 77% after 2033 without changes, so we treat it as a base and build the rest ourselves."
answers: Will Social Security be there for young people?

title: The 4% rule
fact: Researcher William Bengen found in 1994 that withdrawing 4% of a portfolio in year one, then adjusting for inflation, historically lasted at least 30 years. $1 million supports about $40,000 a year.
say: "Using the 4% rule, $800,000 supports about $32,000 a year, and Social Security covers the rest."
answers: How much can our client safely spend in retirement?
How do we make sure they don't run out of money?

title: Required minimum distributions at 73
fact: Owners of traditional IRAs and 401(k)s must start taking required minimum distributions at age 73 (75 for people born in 1960 or later). Roth IRAs have no RMDs for the original owner.
say: "A Roth IRA never forces you to withdraw, so it can keep growing tax-free for your heirs."
answers: Roth or traditional for a client thinking about heirs?

title: Estate and gift limits for 2027
fact: The federal estate and lifetime gift exemption is $15 million per person for 2026 and $15.48 million for 2027. The annual gift exclusion rises from $19,000 to $20,000 per recipient in 2027.
say: "Very few families owe estate tax, but every family needs a will, a guardian and updated beneficiaries."
answers: Do our clients need to worry about estate tax?
Why do young parents need estate planning?

title: Prince died without a will
fact: When Prince died in 2016 with no will, his estate took about six years and long court battles to settle. Aretha Franklin left handwritten wills, one found in her couch; a jury decided in 2023 which one counted.
say: "Prince's estate took six years to settle because he had no will. A simple will now spares your family that."
answers: What happens if someone dies without a will?

title: Household debt hits $19.1 trillion
fact: U.S. household debt reached $19.1 trillion in the third quarter of 2026, and credit card balances hit a record $1.29 trillion, up $22 billion in three months.
say: "Americans owe a record $1.29 trillion on credit cards, so a plan that keeps you out of that statistic is worth a lot."
source: New York Fed Household Debt and Credit Report (Nov. 10, 2026)
answers: How serious is credit card debt for consumers?

title: The average credit card rate is about 22%
fact: Banks charged an average of 22.36% on credit card accounts that paid interest in the third quarter of 2026. At that rate, a $5,000 balance costs about $1,100 a year in interest.
say: "Paying off a 22% card is a guaranteed 22% return, better than any investment we could recommend."
answers: Should our client pay off debt or invest first?
How expensive is carrying a balance?

title: Student loan rates for 2026-27
fact: Federal Direct loans first disbursed from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027 carry fixed rates of 6.52% for undergraduates, 8.07% for graduate students and 9.07% for Parent PLUS.
say: "Federal undergraduate loans are fixed at 6.52% this year, cheaper and safer than most private loans."
answers: Federal or private student loans?
How should a family pay for college?

title: The 2027-28 FAFSA opened early; Grad PLUS ended
fact: The 2027-28 FAFSA opened in late September 2026, its earliest launch ever. Starting July 1, 2026, new Grad PLUS loans ended and new borrowing caps apply to graduate and Parent PLUS loans.
say: "File the FAFSA now. It's already open, and some aid is first come, first served."
source: Federal Student Aid; U.S. Department of Education
answers: When should a family apply for financial aid?

title: GDP grew 3.4% last quarter
fact: Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter of 2026, up from 2.2% in the second quarter, according to the advance estimate.
say: "The economy is growing at 3.4%, a good time to build reserves before the next slowdown."
answers: How is the economy doing right now?
How should the plan change if a recession hits?

title: Unemployment is 4.1%
fact: Employers added 165,000 jobs in October 2026 and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%.
say: "With unemployment at 4.1%, jobs are fairly secure now, which is exactly when to fill the emergency fund."
answers: Which economic indicator would you watch?

title: Inflation peaked at 9.1% in 2022
fact: CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, the highest in about 40 years, which led the Fed to raise rates from near zero to 5.25%-5.50% by July 2023.
say: "In 2022 inflation hit 9.1%. Cash that earned nothing lost almost a tenth of its value in one year."
answers: Why shouldn't our client keep everything in cash?

title: The $9.6 trillion-a-day currency market
fact: The foreign exchange market traded about $9.6 trillion a day in April 2025, and the U.S. dollar was on one side of about 89% of trades.
say: "Currency markets trade almost $10 trillion a day, so exchange rates move fast, which is why an exporter should hedge."
source: Bank for International Settlements Triennial Survey (2025)
answers: How does a strong dollar affect a business that sells overseas?

title: 4,238 FDIC-insured banks
fact: There were 4,238 FDIC-insured institutions in the second quarter of 2026, down 41 in the quarter, and more than 17,000 in 1984. U.S. banks earned $90.1 billion that quarter.
say: "There are about a quarter as many banks as in 1984, so a local institution that knows you is worth seeking out."
answers: How does consolidation affect customers?
How do banks make money?

title: Goodbye, penny
fact: The U.S. Mint struck its last pennies for circulation in November 2025 because each cost about 3.7 cents to make. Existing pennies remain legal tender.
say: "Even money itself changes: the penny cost almost four cents to make, so the government stopped producing it."
answers: What is money, and how is it changing?

title: Cash is now 1 in 7 payments
fact: Cash was used for about 14% of U.S. consumer payments in 2024, down from about 31% in 2016; cards and electronic payments make up most of the rest.
say: "Most payments are digital now, which is why online account security belongs in every plan."
source: Federal Reserve Diary of Consumer Payment Choice
answers: How do people pay for things today?

title: 5.6 million unbanked households
fact: About 4.2% of U.S. households (5.6 million) had no bank account in 2023. The top reason given was not having enough money to meet minimum balance requirements.
say: "A no-minimum checking account at a credit union gets you out of check-cashing fees, which can cost hundreds a year."
source: FDIC National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households (2023)
answers: How would you help a client who doesn't have a bank account?

title: Report debit fraud within 2 days
fact: Under Regulation E, if you report an unauthorized debit card or electronic transfer within 2 business days, your loss is capped at $50; within 60 days, $500; after that it can be unlimited.
say: "Turn on instant alerts. If you report a fraudulent debit within two business days, the most you can lose is $50."
answers: How often should our client check their accounts?

title: Payday loans cost about 400% APR
fact: A typical two-week payday loan with a $15 fee per $100 borrowed equals an APR of almost 400%, and many borrowers roll loans over repeatedly.
say: "A $15 fee on $100 for two weeks sounds small, but it's about a 400% APR. A credit union small-dollar loan is far cheaper."
answers: Why not use a payday loan in an emergency?

title: FBI: $20.9 billion lost to internet crime
fact: The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center counted about $20.9 billion in reported losses for 2025, up about 26% from 2024. Investment fraud, much of it crypto-related, was the costliest category.
say: "Online fraud losses keep setting records, so we'd build scam protection into your plan from day one."
answers: How big a problem is fraud?

title: A $25 million deepfake
fact: In 2024 an employee at engineering firm Arup's Hong Kong office sent about $25 million after a video call in which the 'executives' were AI deepfakes.
say: "AI can fake a voice or a face, so we'd set a family code word and a rule: verify any money request by calling a number you already know."
answers: What are the risks of AI in finance?
How would you protect a client from scams?

title: The IRS Identity Protection PIN
fact: Anyone who can verify their identity can get an IRS Identity Protection PIN, a six-digit number required to file a return in their name, which blocks fraudulent tax filings.
say: "An IRS IP PIN takes ten minutes to set up and stops anyone else from filing a tax return in your name."
answers: Our client's identity was stolen. What now?

title: The $53 million small-town theft
fact: Rita Crundwell, comptroller of Dixon, Illinois, stole about $53 million over two decades through a secret account. She was caught when a coworker covering her vacation noticed it.
say: "Mandatory vacations sound minor, but that's how a $53 million theft was finally caught."
answers: How would you prevent employee theft?

title: TD Bank's $3 billion guilty plea
fact: In October 2024 TD Bank pleaded guilty to Bank Secrecy Act violations and agreed to pay about $3 billion, the largest such penalty against a U.S. bank; most of its transactions had gone unmonitored for years.
say: "Compliance isn't optional. TD Bank paid about $3 billion because it didn't monitor transactions."
answers: Isn't regulation just extra cost?
How do banks stop money laundering?

title: The $2 billion texting crackdown
fact: From 2021 to 2024 the SEC and CFTC fined dozens of financial firms more than $2 billion combined because employees used unapproved apps like WhatsApp for business and the messages weren't kept.
say: "Every business message must be recorded, which is why our firm uses approved, archived channels only."
answers: How can technology help a firm stay compliant?

title: The GENIUS Act for stablecoins
fact: The GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025, created the first federal rules for payment stablecoins, including 1-to-1 reserves in cash or short-term Treasuries and regular disclosures.
say: "Stablecoins now have federal rules, but they're still not FDIC-insured deposits, so we treat them differently from a bank account."
answers: Is crypto regulated?
Should our client invest in crypto?

title: Form CRS: the plain-English summary
fact: Since June 30, 2020, brokers and investment advisers must give retail clients Form CRS, a short summary of services, fees, conflicts of interest and disciplinary history.
say: "Here's our Form CRS: two pages showing every fee and conflict, so you know exactly how we're paid."
answers: What are your responsibilities to us?
How can we trust you?

title: The CrowdStrike outage
fact: In July 2024 a faulty CrowdStrike software update crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers, grounding flights; Delta said the outage cost it about $500 million.
say: "One vendor's bad update shut down airlines, so we'd plan for technology failure with backups and business interruption coverage."
answers: What's the biggest risk to this business?
How would you manage third-party risk?

title: Break-even for a food truck
fact: With $6,000 of monthly fixed costs, a $12 average meal and $5 of variable cost, each meal contributes $7, so break-even is about 857 meals a month, roughly 29 a day.
say: "You break even at about 29 meals a day. Everything after that is profit."
source: Break-even formula: fixed costs / contribution margin
answers: How many sales does the business need to break even?

title: Toys R Us and too much debt
fact: Toys R Us was bought in a 2005 leveraged buyout that left it with about $5 billion of debt. Interest payments starved it of money to modernize, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2017.
say: "Debt has to be repaid in good months and bad. Toys R Us showed what happens when a business borrows too much."
answers: Should the business take a loan or an investor?
Is all debt bad?

title: Spanx: started with $5,000
fact: Sara Blakely started Spanx with $5,000 of her own savings and kept full ownership for years by bootstrapping, before selling a majority stake in 2021 at a $1.2 billion valuation.
say: "Bootstrapping kept 100% of Spanx with its founder. Growing on your own revenue first keeps your options open."
answers: How should this business raise money?
What makes a successful entrepreneur?

title: Record new business applications
fact: Americans have filed more than 5 million new business applications each year since 2021, well above pre-pandemic levels.
say: "Entrepreneurship is booming, which also means more competition, so your plan needs a clear edge."
source: U.S. Census Bureau Business Formation Statistics
answers: Is now a good time to start a business?

title: A data breach costs $4.4 million
fact: The average cost of a data breach was about $4.4 million globally in 2025.
say: "If you store customer data, cyber insurance and two-factor logins aren't optional. One breach can cost more than the business is worth."
source: IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025
answers: What insurance should this business buy?

title: Egg prices and the price variance
fact: Repeated bird-flu outbreaks from 2022 to 2025 pushed wholesale egg prices to records, giving bakeries and restaurants large unfavorable materials price variances. Many responded with menu changes or surcharges.
say: "Your food costs are over budget because of egg prices, a price variance, so the fix is the supplier or the menu, not the staff."
source: USDA and BLS price data; news reports
answers: How would you track whether the business sticks to its budget?

title: WorldCom's $3.8 billion trick
fact: WorldCom recorded about $3.8 billion of ordinary expenses as assets to inflate profit. The fraud, uncovered in 2002, helped bring about the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
say: "WorldCom shows why profit alone can mislead. We'd read all four statements, not just the income statement."
answers: Which financial statement matters most?
What would you do if asked to make the numbers look better?

title: Flood isn't in your homeowners policy
fact: Standard homeowners policies don't cover flood damage. Flood coverage comes from the National Flood Insurance Program or private insurers. Hurricane Helene in 2024 flooded inland areas where few homeowners had it.
say: "Your home policy won't pay for a flood. A separate flood policy is cheap where risk seems low, which is exactly where Helene hit."
answers: What insurance does a homeowner need?

title: Insurers retreat from wildfire zones
fact: Allstate (2022) and State Farm (2023) stopped writing new home policies in California, and the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires were among the costliest disasters in U.S. history.
say: "Insurance gets harder to buy where risk is rising, so we'd review coverage limits every year and price that into the home decision."
answers: How does climate risk affect insurance?

title: Most active funds trail the index
fact: Roughly 9 in 10 actively managed U.S. large-cap stock funds trailed the S&P 500 over 15 years, according to S&P's SPIVA scorecard.
say: "Even professionals rarely beat the index for long, so a low-cost index fund puts the odds on your side."
source: S&P Dow Jones Indices SPIVA U.S. Scorecard
answers: Why an index fund instead of picking stocks?

title: 2022: stocks and bonds fell together
fact: In 2022 the S&P 500 lost about 18% and the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index about 13%, a rare year when bonds didn't cushion stock losses, because rising rates hit both.
say: "Even bonds can fall when rates jump, which is why we match investments to your timeline, not just mix stocks and bonds."
answers: Why do bond prices fall when rates rise?
How do you decide how much risk the client takes?

title: Spot bitcoin ETFs
fact: The SEC approved the first spot bitcoin ETFs in January 2024, letting investors hold bitcoin exposure in ordinary brokerage accounts. Bitcoin's price still fell more than 60% in 2022.
say: "If you want crypto, a regulated bitcoin ETF capped at about 5% of your investments limits the damage if it crashes."
answers: Should our client invest in crypto?

title: OpenAI's five-day board crisis
fact: In November 2023 OpenAI's nonprofit board fired CEO Sam Altman, then reinstated him within days after employees and investors pushed back, a case study in how governance structure shapes control.
say: "Who controls the board decides who controls the company, which is why we'd set clear governance before taking on investors."
answers: Why does corporate governance matter?

title: Keeping clients pays
fact: Bain & Company research found that raising customer retention by 5% can raise profits by 25% to 95%, because loyal customers buy more, cost less to serve and refer others.
say: "Keeping a client is far cheaper than finding a new one, so our CRM schedules a check-in before every big date in your life."
answers: How would you keep this client relationship strong?
